sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to this explainer.
Since most servers in the world run on Linux, it is very important that we understand rather than guess.
Because the real difference between being lost on a night the server is down and knowing and controlling everything that happens starts here.
In this explainer we will understand the basics and concepts that build this system piece by piece, so we are in control of every detail.
Let us get right into it.
Our journey is split into six stations: permissions and files, users and groups, processes and resources, packages and software, reading, search and networking, and finally a hands-on lab.
The first station, the foundation: permissions and files.
There is an important question here that will show us how the system thinks.
Have you ever asked yourselves why sometimes we give a group a certain permission and find that nothing changed, as if we did nothing?
The secret lies in how the kernel thinks.
Imagine it as a strict gatekeeper facing three people, each with keys: read r, write w and execute x.
This guard asks his questions in order: first, is this person the owner?
If yes, he applies the owner permissions and stops asking; he does not even look at the group.
If not, he moves to the second question: is he in the group? And so on.
That is why group permissions can be ignored completely if the user turns out to be the owner from the start.
Okay, what is the story with these keys?
They are simply the bricks we build any permission from.
Each permission has a fixed number that never changes.
Read: we give it the letter r and the number 4.
Write: its letter is w and its number is 2.
Execute: its letter is x and its number is 1.
And if there is no permission at all, it is a minus sign and its number is 0.
The nice thing about this system is that we simply add these numbers up.
So to give a permission like 755, for the owner we add 4, 2, 1 to get 7; for the group 4 and 1 make 5; and for the rest also 4 and 1, so 5.
So now we understand 755, which we use for folders and scripts.
What about 644? That is the normal one for files: the owner reads and writes, 4 plus 2 is 6, and the rest only read, so 4 and 4.
And we have 700 for private keys.
But watch out: this 777 carries a huge warning sign, because it means anyone can do anything, and that is a disaster.
No respectable work environment uses it as a solution.
Let us see this in practice.
We wrote a perfectly fine script and run it with dot slash hello.sh, and oops, we get the annoying message Permission denied.
Before we rush, we must diagnose the problem first: we type the command ls -l.
We find that the letter x, the execute permission, is missing.
The fix is simply the command chmod +x hello.sh.
And with that we have solved the problem, whether we use numbers or letters with chmod.
But an important question: where do these default permissions come from?
The system starts from 666 for files and 777 for folders, then subtracts a value called the umask.
So if the umask is 022, the result is 644 for files and 755 for folders.
Try for example touch private.txt with umask 077: you will find the file created with permission 600, locked tight against everyone but the owner.
And of course, to change a file's owner or group, chown does the job, and chgrp if it is only the group.
Our second station is users and groups, or we could say the system's identity.
Identity management in Linux has essential commands you cannot do without.
whoami tells the system who we are right now, and id fetches the details.
And here our eyes always go to root, whose number is zero and which has all permissions.
We create a new user with sudo useradd -m -s and set its password with passwd.
And here is an extremely dangerous warning.
When we add a user to an existing group with usermod -aG, never forget the letter a.
If you forget it, the user will be thrown out of all their old groups in a second.
And when we want to delete a user completely, we use userdel -r.
All this data is recorded in the file /etc/passwd.
But the passwords are encrypted and safely hidden in the file /etc/shadow, which no one but root can read.
The third station: processes and resources, and how to run our server properly.
Any process in the world is simply a running program.
If we look at the output of ps aux, we see this table connected to live counters moving in front of us for CPU and memory.
These counters are what reveal who is eating the server's resources.
Of course we can use interactive commands that sort these processes, like top and htop, to catch the culprit quickly.
Okay, we found the culprit and want to stop it: here we send signals to the program.
If we use kill -15, it sends a SIGTERM signal, which we consider a very polite request.
It lets the program close its files, clean up after itself and exit gracefully.
On the other hand, kill -9 sends SIGKILL, and that is the hard hit: it shuts the program down immediately.
And it may leave damaged files behind, so we keep it as the very last resort.
There is also the SIGHUP signal, 1, which tells the program: please re-read your settings, without stopping.
To make life easier we can use commands like killall, pkill and pgrep.
Sometimes we have heavy tasks that we do not want tying up the screen.
The fix is to put the ampersand at the end of the command, and that throws the task into the background.
We can follow it with jobs and move it freely between fg and bg.
We can also give it a CPU priority with nice, which runs from minus 20 as the highest priority to 19 as the lowest.
And if it is already running or we want to change its priority, we use renice.
And to be at ease and make sure the task keeps running even if we close the screen or log out, we prefix it with nohup.
The fourth station: packages and software, installing and removing.
When we remove a program there is a huge difference between deleting it and wiping it out of existence.
apt remove removes the program but keeps its settings, so if we change our minds and reinstall it we find our stuff ready.
But apt purge deletes literally everything: the program, its settings, its files, everything.
And of course we know the basics, like apt update to refresh the index, apt upgrade to update the programs themselves, and apt install to download new programs.
And if we want to go a bit lower level and deal with the package itself, we use the dpkg tool.
We move to the fifth station: tools for reading, search and networking.
These are the things we use every day.
To read big log files without the machine freezing, the less command is the perfect solution.
And if we want to watch the log live, line by line as it is being written, we use tail -f.
If we are searching for something precisely, find is very powerful and has tons of filters.
While locate is much faster, but it relies on a database that may not be up to date at that moment.
And we have which to know exactly where commands are located.
When we need to edit files, we either use the simple nano or the mighty vim.
And by the way, to save and exit it we type a colon and then wq.
A server's health is always measured by its disk space and its network.
We make shortcuts to files with ln -s and compress the work with tar -czvf.
Our eyes should always be on the df -h command.
As soon as we find its usage has passed 80%, it is an emergency that needs immediate attention.
Then we use du to find out which folders are eating the space.
As for networking, ip addr gets the IP and ping reassures us about the connection.
And ss -tulnp reveals who has a port open and running.
Not to mention quick, important rescue tools like curl and dig.
We have reached the sixth and final station, the hands-on lab, where we tie everything together in a shared team folder.
Imagine with us a team that needs a shared folder.
The first step: we create a group with sudo groupadd webteam.
The second step: we add users like alice and bob to this group.
Then we give the group ownership of the folder with chown root:webteam.
The whole trick and the magic is in the next step: chmod 2775.
The 2 at the start is what we call the SGID bit, and it does a great move.
It forces any new file created inside the folder to automatically take the folder's group.
So all team members can work on and edit each other's files smoothly, without anyone locking the work away from the other.
These basics we have seen eliminate guesswork in emergencies and keep us understanding and in control of our system with full confidence.
The question now is: after you have acquired these powerful tools, what complex systems will you be able to build, or what workflows will you secure and automate with ease?
That is what we will start to discover together as we progress.
In the next explainer we will continue the journey into the details of services and SSH basics. Thank you very much for watching.
